claim: An integer-class return value is placed in the first available register of the sequence RAX, RDX, so the first eightbyte comes back in RAX.
quote: If the class is INTEGER, the next available register of the sequence \RAX, \RDX is used.

claim: The stack must be 16 bytes aligned (32 or 64 bytes if __m256 or __m512 is passed on the stack) immediately before a call instruction executes.
quote: In other words, the stack needs to be 16 (32 or 64) byte aligned immediately before the call instruction is executed.

claim: For a 64-bit PUSH, the stack pointer is decremented by 8 and the source operand is written at the new top of stack.
For a 64-bit POP, the value at the top of stack is copied to the destination and then the stack pointer is incremented by 8.
quote: DEST := SS:RSP; (* Copy quadword *) RSP := RSP + 8;

claim: For a 64-bit signed divide, RDX:RAX holds the dividend, RAX receives the quotient and RDX receives the remainder.
quote: In 64-bit mode when REX.W is applied, the instruction divides the signed value in RDX:RAX by the source operand. RAX contains a 64-bit quotient; RDX contains a 64-bit remainder.

claim: CQO, available only in 64-bit mode, copies the sign (bit 63) of RAX into every bit position of RDX.
quote: The CQO instruction (available in 64-bit mode only) copies the sign (bit 63) of the value in the RAX register into every bit position in the RDX register.

claim: IDIV signals the #DE divide-error exception when the divisor is 0 or when the signed quotient is too large for the destination register.
quote: If the source operand (divisor) is 0. The signed result (quotient) is too large for the destination.

claim: On x86 Linux, the #DE divide error is handled by sending SIGFPE with si_code FPE_INTDIV to the process.
quote: do_error_trap(regs, 0, "divide error", X86_TRAP_DE, SIGFPE, FPE_INTDIV, error_get_trap_addr(regs));

locator: section 9.16.3.1 AT&T Syntax versus Intel Syntax
claim: In AT&T syntax the operands are written source first and destination second, the opposite order from Intel syntax.
quote: AT&T and Intel syntax use the opposite order for source and destination operands. Intel ‘add eax, 4’ is ‘addl $4, %eax’. The ‘source, dest’ convention is maintained for compatibility with previous Unix assemblers.

locator: section 9.16.3.1 AT&T Syntax versus Intel Syntax
claim: GNU as uses AT&T syntax by default; Intel syntax is selected only with the .intel_syntax directive.
quote: as now supports assembly using Intel assembler syntax. .intel_syntax selects Intel mode, and .att_syntax switches back to the usual AT&T mode for compatibility with the output of gcc.
